item.title: Re: "Long" Beach California (Seeking Feedback)
item.content:encoded:
Hey there BUCKSHOT74, I’ll be critting your idea today!
Note that I am not an official reviewer, so take what I say with a grain of salt. With that said, let’s begin the crit!

+ Open Section-by-Section
Woooooosh

Elevator Pitch

So it’s a beach 60 miles1 south of Long Beach where the water seems 80-90 yards2 away, yet never gets closer. To be honest, I’m not too keen on this idea (by itself). It isn’t very interesting in my opinion (all it is is a beach where the water doesn’t get closer), and seems to simply be the opposite of SCP-2684. However, if a good narrative is applied to it, it still could work.

Central Narrative

The narrative here consists of the Foundation sending out people to find out what’s up with the beach, and that’s about it. Some people die, they find some writing (which you proceed to not tell us about), and there’s a vague notion of a tall, mysterious entity that kills everyone who saw it. Personally, I don’t really like this. There isn’t any deeper narrative or explanation as to why the beach appeared, it just boils down to people being killed, which I find uninteresting.

Hook/Attention Grabber

The dry-drowning premise is unique[…]

Unfortunately, it isn’t. SCP-1812 is an excellent example of a dry-drowning premise that is in-theme, where we see the dry-drowning is due to the perceived higher gravitational pull on Earth’s water. In your idea, we don’t have an explanation as to why the first D-Class suddenly drowned, they just did. Oddly, they drowned at 8kms out rather than much sooner (which would make sense with the water depths of the average beach), and I’d like an explanation.

Also, as I explained earlier, the narrative is kind of boring, so the audio logs wouldn’t keep the reader entertained.

+ Open General Thoughts
I don’t know about this

The idea is (in my opinion) relatively boring, the narrative isn’t interesting and doesn’t give any explanation for the beach or entity, and the unique concept in your hook isn’t unique. Unless you overhaul the narrative to this, I don’t think your concept would survive on the mainsite.

Anyway, that’s it for my crit today. Thanks for reading, and I hope this helps!

Footnotes
1. Metric, not imperial, is the system used on the Site.
2. Metric.

item.title: Re: The Infinite Beach (Seeking Greenlights)
item.content:encoded:
Hey! Thanks for the feedback! Your understanding of this SCP is totally correct. Also, thank you, as your questions have pointed out some weaknesses in my world-building, and I'm definitely going to expand on these in the next draft.

To answer your questions:

+ show block
– hide block

1. Day and night progress in the SCP's area of affect in parallel with reality.
2. I want to say steel, but I realize now that 26 km of steel cable is going to be very heavy. I'm either going to have to change the distances or rethink the recovery method.
3. It's a separate reality pocket that exists outside the euclidean geometry of the real world. I'm going to need to make it have an entrance and defined parameters.
4. If you mean using drones or something like that to explore, no, and I don't intend to do so. If you mean civilians are the first to stumble across the SCP, I suppose that's a good way to establish the SCP's origins. I may try that too.
5. Randomly Occurring

item.title: Re: The Infinite Beach (Seeking Greenlights)
item.content:encoded:
I dont have the authority to greenlight, but your idea for an SCP is very cool. So Let me get this straight you can continue walking but you won't get any closer to the water and at a certain time you will drown even though there is no water.

Just a quick couple of questions

  1. Is there a day and night cycle within the SCP?
  2. What are the tethers made out of?
  3. Is this SCP a distortion of reality or something else entirely?
  4. Has there been and autonomous expedition of your SCP?
  5. Is it made by something or just randomly occurring?

item.title: "Long" Beach California (Seeking Feedback)
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre (Optional): N/A

Page Layout (Optional): Standard SCP Article. Name, Classification, Containment procedures, description.

Elevator Pitch: This SCP is a beach sixty miles south of Long Beach, California upon which, no matter how far on walks, the water can never be reached, yet always appears to be no more than eighty to ninety yards away.

+ show block
– hide block

Central Narrative: Through audio logs between expeditionary personnel and command, readers will follow teams of research personnel sent to explore SCP-XXXX in hopes to discover more about its anomalous nature. The first audio log reveals initial exploration results in a casualty around eight km out. Autopsy reveals cause of death to be asphyxia by drowning. The second log reveals that use of a SCBA allows explorers to venture out substantially farther, reaching close to sixteen kilometers before oxygen tanks reach half-way empty and they must turn around. The third log follows a team of researchers equipped with oxygen tanks that last eighteen hours. The team reports around thirty km out that there is some form of writing in the sand. Later, they report what they believe to be a boat in the distance, floating offshore. At thirty-nine km, three of the oxygen tanks simultaneously malfunction. The team turns around, holding their breath unless breathing through the SCBA, which they must share. All team members are recovered, and the writing in the sand is sent to linguists for deciphering. The final log documents the exploration of four research personnel on board a semi-aquatic vehicle designed to withstand high pressure and impact. They make it twenty-six km before the vehicle begins to flood with water. The team is forced to abandon the vehicle and carry on. At the fifty-seven km mark, the lead researcher calls in that there appears to be a tall, disproportionate figure down near the water, henceforth denoted as SCP-XXXX-1. Before command can respond, all exploration personnel experience simultaneous SCBA failures, and the hissing of air and screaming of researchers can be heard before comm connection is lost. Three of the four corpses are recovered and autopsied, and cause of death is determined to be asphyxia by drowning. The fourth cable comes back severed, and there is blood and a torn shred of clothing on the cable.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: The dry-drowning premise is unique and the audio logs will serve to keep readers interested.

Additional Notes: Researchers in the audio logs are tethered by spools of steel cable so they can be recovered. Feedback still welcome.
